turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: We will hear argument this morning in Case 25-581, St. Mary Catholic Parish versus Roy. Mr. Reaves.

turns.name: NICHOLAS R. REAVES
turns.text: Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court: The Archdiocese of Denver schools exist to pass on the faith to the next generation. To do this, they ask all families who enroll to be open to and supportive of the church's teachings. Because of this sincere religious exercise, the State has denied Colorado families the ability to use Universal Preschool funding at Catholic schools. Under this Court's public benefits cases, that triggers strict scrutiny. The Tenth Circuit was wrong to cabin that precedent that this Court reaffirmed in Carson to explicit religious exclusions only. That can't be reconciled with Sherbert, Thomas, or Mahmoud. Nor can it be reconciled with this Court's instruction in Carson to look to the operation and the effect of the law, not for magic words. After rejecting Carson, the Tenth Circuit applied Smith, but this too was wrong. When Colorado allows over a thousand schools to turn families away for a variety of different reasons, it has created a flexible and customizable program, nothing like the generally applicable across-the-board laws that Smith envisioned. And Colorado's inconsistent and contradictory arguments further confirm the state's actions are anything but generally applicable. Colorado has flexibly interpreted the mandate to accommodate important secular interests, but it's called the same law a hard limit when Petitioners sought a religious accommodation. And Colorado has discretion via the catch-all exemption to permit preschools to organize around "specific competencies or interests" and to serve "specific communities." Yet it has refused to extend that flexible treatment to Petitioners. Finally, this is not a zero-sum game. Letting families use Universal Preschool funding at Catholic schools won't take away a single seat from the over 2,000 preschools already participating in the program. In fact, letting Catholic schools in will create more seats for everyone, even for families who disagree with Catholic teachings. I welcome the Court's questions.

turns.name: CLARENCE THOMAS
turns.text: Do you think your -- this case is on all fours with Carson, or would we have to extend Carson?

turns.name: NICHOLAS R. REAVES
turns.text: I think the rule this Court applied in Carson when it discussed Sherbert and Thomas is on all fours with this case. Both Sherbert and Thomas involved facially neutral laws, and that's my understanding of where this Court derived the public benefits rule it applied in Carson. I would also look to the holding that this Court articulated at the end of its opinion in Carson, which says, "Regardless of how the benefit and restriction are described, the program operates to identify and exclude otherwise eligible schools on the basis of their religious exercise." So that's how I understand this Court's decision in Carson. And I also think the focus of the way that this Court resolved Carson was to look at, you know, what is happening to the religious believer? It didn't focus on the text of the law in Maine. It focused on whether schools are being excluded on account of their religious exercise.

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: But I --

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: But --

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: -- I'm a little confused. I'm sorry, Chief, go ahead.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: -- Carson was third in a line of cases, you know, Trinity Lutheran, Espinoza, and then Carson. The law in those cases, in each of them, expressly discriminated against religious schools on its face. That's not the case here. Shouldn't that make a significant difference given the potential reach of the principle you're asking for?

turns.name: NICHOLAS R. REAVES
turns.text: Your Honor, a few points. I don't think we're actually asking for a very broad principle. And I think it is the principle that this Court articulated previously in Sherbert and Thomas and then reaffirmed in Mahmoud. In all three of those cases, the law on its face was neutral. But, to also talk about the scope of this rule, when we're talking about public benefits, it's -- it's a relatively small category of things we're talking about. This Court has applied the public benefits precedent when we're talking about welfare benefits and education funding predominantly, and I don't think this rule would -- would change much beyond that.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Well, just to interrupt for a moment, would it not in your view apply to things like drivers' licenses, employment benefits, Social Security? I'm not quite sure how you limit the applicability of your principle.

turns.name: NICHOLAS R. REAVES
turns.text: Yeah. Your Honor, I think it would apply to situations where the government is subsidizing private conduct. A license, for example, would not be a public benefit because that's the government using its regulatory power. So I think that would be more akin to, you know, maybe you would apply a different Free Exercise Clause principle like Smith. But my read of the public benefits cases is that the underlying conduct has to be something you can do already and we're just talking about the government subsidizing private conduct. In -- in this Court's Everson decision, it described the rule as the ben -- as "the benefits of public welfare legislation." And I think that's kind of the realm of what we're looking at here.

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: What I guess I -- I'm -- I'm trying to understand is what do we do with the fact that not all Catholic schools are being excluded in fact as a result of this rule? I mean, my understanding is that there are many religious schools, that the -- the -- not only does the State seek to have religious schools as a part of this program but that many religious schools even in the same faith have chosen to participate, have followed the mandate. So what -- what do we do with that?

turns.name: NICHOLAS R. REAVES
turns.text: Mm-hmm. Your Honor, I think it's telling that neither of the courts below found the -- the argument compelling. And this is at JA 155. But, essentially, the testimony from the superintendent of Catholic schools was that Catholic Charities, which operates these Head Start programs, which do participate in the program, they have a very different mission and ministry. Their ministry is to serve those most in need. So you can think of that akin to Catholic Charities running a soup kitchen. They don't ask people if they're Catholic.

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: They're the ones that are in the program?

turns.name: NICHOLAS R. REAVES
turns.text: They're the ones that are in the program, Your Honor.

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: Mm-hmm.

turns.name: NICHOLAS R. REAVES
turns.text: And on the flip side, you have parish preschools, and the role of the parish preschools is different. They have a different mission. Their mission is to support parents in the Catholic education of their children. And so they -- they ask all families who seek to enroll to affirm in good faith the statement of community beliefs.

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: But you say that --

turns.name: NICHOLAS R. REAVES
turns.text: So it's just -- it's a different religious --

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: -- that -- but, in response to the Chief Justice, you say that this is about the government subsidizing private conduct. And if we frame it that way, I guess I'm a little concerned that these parish preschools would like to do something that the State has determined is a violation of its own principles with respect to discriminating against or excluding a certain group of people. So why is it -- it that the state can uniformly condition the receipt of these funds on something like you can't discriminate? It seems to me you're asking for a special rule for religious schools, that when Colorado says anyone who receives these funds has to be open to everyone and can't discriminate, what you're asking for in the context of this Free Exercise claim is a special rule for religious schools to be able to not follow that condition. And why -- am I right about that or no?

turns.name: NICHOLAS R. REAVES
turns.text: No, Your Honor.

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: Okay.

turns.name: NICHOLAS R. REAVES
turns.text: So -- so two points. And this does kind of get into some of the general applicability analysis, which I don't think is relevant to the Carson claim. But, at the end of the day, we are seeking the same thing that lots of other schools are allowed to do. Over a thousand other schools participate in the program and that they're --

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: That's not the -- I'm not on the general applicability. I'm on the why is it discrimination -- why is Colorado's intention to have this principle that applies to everyone -- assume for the moment it applies to everyone -- why is it discrimination if the religious schools say we don't want to follow that? And I -- I mean, I sort of thought that's what Smith was doing in -- in its analysis. You -- you have to follow the general rules of the society as long as they're not targeting you on the basis of your religion.

turns.name: NICHOLAS R. REAVES
turns.text: Your Honor, I would make two points.

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: Mm-hmm.

turns.name: NICHOLAS R. REAVES
turns.text: First, the Carson rule is really rooted in Sherbert and Thomas. And the rule -- the argument you're articulating is the same argument that Indiana made in Thomas. They said, you know, these rules apply to everybody. But what this Court said in those cases was, if there's a sincere religious exercise that's being burdened, the government has to show a really good reason for doing that. And in terms of the discrimination here, I actually think --

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: But that's not what we said in Smith, right? It wasn't just the burden. It was that the -- the rule had to be not neutral and not generally applicable. And yet somehow, here, you're suggesting that a rule that applies to all schools doesn't target religion, you can get -- you -- you -- you don't have to follow if it burdens religion. And that's not what -- what I thought our baseline rule was in this area.

turns.name: NICHOLAS R. REAVES
turns.text: Well, Your Honor, my read of this Court's decision in Carson is that it roots the rule in Sherbert and Thomas, not in Smith. And I think the Tenth Circuit was right about one thing. They were right to say -- yes, Justice?

turns.name: ELENA KAGAN
turns.text: But, Mr. Reaves, I mean, going back to the Chief Justice's question, and this may be just a restatement of Justice Jackson, what Carson most was was the third in a line of cases about schools, you know, Trinity Lutheran, Espinoza, Carson, all three of which had explicit exclusions for either religious institutions or religious practice. And -- and whatever is cited there, you know, oh, look, there's a citation to Sherbert, Carson really followed from those two other cases or -- or, you know, the Court understood it that way, and it was a nondiscrimination principle. It was religious people are not being treated the same way as non-religious people here in each of those three cases. And I think what you're asking us to do is something far beyond that. It's saying, even though religious people are being treated the same way -- and this puts aside Question 1 a little bit, you know, where you have some argument on -- on the neutrality front, but -- but I just want to focus on your main argument, which is, even though religious people are being treated the same way on the face of the statute, that's not enough. They need a special accommodation. They need to be treated differently from other people to have a -- a -- a -- because of their religious faith, to have a special accommodation. And that, it seems to me, is very much not what Trinity Lutheran and Espinoza and Carson are about.

turns.name: NICHOLAS R. REAVES
turns.text: Your Honor, I think the problem with limiting Carson in that way is it makes that rule very easy to circumvent. And that was a concern this Court had in Carson itself. It talked about how easy it would be to circumvent the prior cases if it really turned on how the government described the program. So, you know, you can imagine situations where the government is keeping out religious schools, but it's just not using the word "religion" or the word "sectarian." That's the situation --

turns.name: ELENA KAGAN
turns.text: Yeah, it does not seem to me that this is a good case to raise the kind of specter of circumvention. I don't think that there's any idea here or, you know, I think it would be a bit far-fetched to say that the government is doing this surreptitiously to get at religious schools, which I agree, you know, in a case of -- we've had cases of that kind, where it's like, oh, look, they -- they framed it neutrally, but their motive was very clear. I mean, this is a case of the state trying to enforce its own nondiscrimination principles, which it takes deeply seriously, including as applied to sexual orientation. So -- so I don't think that this is kind of like a surreptitious circumvention case. It's a case where you're saying, no, because of religious faith, we need a special exemption, an accommodation, a way of being treated differently with respect to that neutral antidiscrimination principle.

turns.name: NICHOLAS R. REAVES
turns.text: Your Honor, I do think there is a circumvention concern here because the way the program operates, you have over 2300 schools that can limit enrollment for all kinds of reasons. You can have a school that says, we're only going to admit vegetarians who speak two languages. But you won't allow Catholic schools to limit enrollment in this one particular way.

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: I -- I'm sorry --

turns.name: NICHOLAS R. REAVES
turns.text: And the testimony --

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: -- I -- I -- I'm a little confused, okay? The Catholic schools are not being excluded on their face. They're choosing not to participate because they won't get an exemption, correct? So this is their choice.

turns.name: NICHOLAS R. REAVES
turns.text: They're being excluded by Colorado.

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: Well, no, because Colorado permits them to apply if they will accept all children. They're saying, we don't want to accept the children of a certain class of people, homosexual people. So the children are being -- they're not saying -- Colorado is not saying you have to teach equality. It's not saying you have to teach it's okay to be homosexual. You don't have to teach -- change your values in any way. You can teach whatever it is you want to teach, but if parents choose to subject their children to this teaching, you have to accept that child. Is that correct?

turns.name: NICHOLAS R. REAVES
turns.text: Well, Your Honor, for the Catholic Church, it's not about excluding anyone based on who they are. And that is in the record at Pet. App 11a.

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: Well, I don't see how that can be. They're saying, we'll exclude your children if their parents are homosexual.

turns.name: NICHOLAS R. REAVES
turns.text: Your Honor, the --

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: Because their parents are doing something we don't agree with. I thought that's -- you know, you have to accept all children, regardless of their religious -- regardless of their sex, race, national origin, whatever it might be.

turns.name: NICHOLAS R. REAVES
turns.text: Well, Your Honor, I guess, to address that in two ways, you know, one, all families, regardless of who they are, even if they're Catholic, have to agree to the statement of community beliefs in good faith. That's the requirement. And the purpose --

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: I -- I'm not -- I mean, it may be that there are some homosexual parents who would sign that statement. But you're saying, I won't sign -- I won't agree to accept those children. And that's what Colorado is objecting to.

turns.name: NICHOLAS R. REAVES
turns.text: And, Your Honor, it is a case-by-case determination at the end of the -- the day. These families can come and -- I also think it's -- it's telling that, you know, since this program has began and even before this program, families who disagree with the Catholic Church's teachings are not banging down the door to try to enroll in Catholic preschools.

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: I agree with you. But you're -- you want an official statement by the State that I will subsidize you with public money even though -- because I have a right to reject children.

turns.name: NICHOLAS R. REAVES
turns.text: Well, Your Honor, at the end of --

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: That's what they're saying. That's what the equal opportunity clause is requiring you to not do, which is to say, I will take all children with these characteristics.

turns.name: NICHOLAS R. REAVES
turns.text: And, Your Honor, at the end of the day, this is a benefit for families. This is not a benefit that goes to the school. This is a per capita benefit. And -- and the government itself is the one telling --

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: So why shouldn't the family have that choice --

turns.name: NICHOLAS R. REAVES
turns.text: Well, I -- I think --

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: -- of saying -- I mean, I'm -- I'm hard-pressed to think that given those teachings that any homosexual family is going to choose to go to one of these schools, but that should be their choice, not your choice to exclude them.

turns.name: NICHOLAS R. REAVES
turns.text: Well, Your Honor, I think --

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: That's what you're asking for.

turns.name: NICHOLAS R. REAVES
turns.text: Your Honor, I think we're asking for these Catholic schools to have the same access as others. And if we're talking about who is being harmed here --

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: They do.

turns.name: NICHOLAS R. REAVES
turns.text: -- the harm is --

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: They just can't exclude children of homosexual parents.

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: Mr. Reaves, would it violate Colorado's policy for you to continue to employ the kind of statement Justice Sotomayor is referring to, the one that you have that requires families to say that they will abide by and support the church's teachings on matters of sexuality and gender?

turns.name: NICHOLAS R. REAVES
turns.text: My understanding is Colorado's interpreted it that way. That's been the policy. You know, Dawn Odean, who's the Respondent in this case, sat through the trial testimony, and we asked her on cross-examination -- this is at JA 333 -- what's the problem, why can't these Catholic schools participate? And her answer was, the barrier is the mandate. So -- and she compared their religious practices to bullying and stigmatization. So it -- it's Colorado that's saying, you know, you are not providing --

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: But -- but I guess my question is even more specific. I -- I'm -- is the problem that the church is saying or that St. Mary's and the diocese is saying, we want affirmatively to turn away families, you know, same-sex couples, you know, whose children want to enroll or a child that's transgender -- may I, Chief Justice?

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Certainly, yeah.

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: Or is it -- or is the problem with the statement? Like, could you use just the statement? Would the statement kind of serve your end? Because, as Justice Sotomayor is saying, it's kind of hard to imagine that couples that disagree with the church's teaching will want to enroll their children in the diocesan schools.

turns.name: NICHOLAS R. REAVES
turns.text: So, in all instances, the family has to sign the statement. But the testimony from trial included testimony from the superintendent saying there would be some circumstances where enrollment would not be possible, and that might be some circumstances involving a same-sex couple. The -- the Diocese has issued guidance to address these situations. That's at Pet. App 242a. So it's not -- it's not a categorical rule. That's what the Tenth Circuit said. But there would be circumstances where they could not guarantee families an equal opportunity to enroll regardless of those protected characteristics. I also do just want to briefly flag we're talking about religion as well. So the congregation exemption was removed, so now these Catholic schools cannot even say we want to prefer Catholics in our enrollment.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Thank you, counsel. Just to follow up to make sure I followed the answer to the line of questioning there, if you had same-sex parents and they wanted their child to go to the school and they said, look, we're not going to contest the school's teachings, we're not going to bring it up, and so we -- would -- would they be eligible for participation, or is it simply the existence of the -- of the couple as opposed to whether or not they would contest the church's teachings?

turns.name: NICHOLAS R. REAVES
turns.text: So, generally, it's the same requirement for everybody. And I think it's telling that this hasn't arisen. But, to answer --

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: I'm sorry. Why -- I'm not sure -- you mean the same requirement for all same-sex couples regardless of what their views on the --

turns.name: NICHOLAS R. REAVES
turns.text: It's --

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: What -- yeah.

turns.name: NICHOLAS R. REAVES
turns.text: I'm sorry. It's the same requirement for all families who seek to enroll. It's to affirm in good faith the statement of community beliefs. And these situations haven't really arisen, so it's a little bit hypothetical. This has never happened at St. Mary's. But the process is the same for everybody. They meet with the principal. They meet with the pastor. They get to learn about the school. But I do think the testimony in the record is clear there are some instances where the Catholic school would have to say we cannot enroll you. And it wouldn't -- you know, it would be because the school cannot affirm things like a same-sex marriage. It's the same policy at the end of the day as Catholic Social Services. They can't endorse or affirm a same-sex marriage. And that might be required in the classroom.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Thank you. Justice Thomas, anything further? Justice Alito?

turns.name: SAMUEL ALITO
turns.text: Well, let me also return to the question of what exactly is required. Is the rule that couples must or parents must affirm certain beliefs about sex and sexuality and -- and that's it, they must sincerely affirm those beliefs, and in determining whether they have sincerely affirmed those beliefs, it would be taken into account whether they are openly living in violation of those beliefs? Is that a correct understanding of it?

turns.name: NICHOLAS R. REAVES
turns.text: I do think that is a correct understanding. It has to be affirmed in good faith. And that -- that could be a problem.

turns.name: SAMUEL ALITO
turns.text: Now, on the circumvention question, I take it there would be a problem if the Colorado law said we will not approve Catholic pre-K. That would be a problem, right?

turns.name: NICHOLAS R. REAVES
turns.text: Yes.

turns.name: SAMUEL ALITO
turns.text: And would it be a -- a problem if the law said we will not approve any pre-K school that requires affirmation of Catholic teaching on sex and sexuality, if it did that explicitly?

turns.name: NICHOLAS R. REAVES
turns.text: I think that would be a problem as well, yes.

turns.name: SAMUEL ALITO
turns.text: And if that's a problem, then could the State get around that by saying that every pre-K school must accept students whose parents reject the principle that marriage is between a man and a woman? That would make no explicit reference to religion.

turns.name: NICHOLAS R. REAVES
turns.text: I think, under the Tenth Circuit's understanding of Carson, that would be okay because it's not explicit.

turns.name: SAMUEL ALITO
turns.text: And in adopting such a rule, is it conceivable that the lawmakers would not understand what the effect of this would be on Catholic pre-K and on pre-K schools affiliated with other religions that adhere to that traditional principle?

turns.name: NICHOLAS R. REAVES
turns.text: I -- I think they would have to know. And I do think they knew in this case. Just to point to one piece of testimony, I'd look at JA 233, and that's where -- where Ms. Cooke testified that the St. Mary's preschool director participated in the working group, and she knew exactly what the problems were when they were developing these preferences.

turns.name: SAMUEL ALITO
turns.text: Thank you.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Justice Sotomayor?

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: Your bottom line is -- let's get to it -- your school can reject a child because their parents are homosexual?

turns.name: NICHOLAS R. REAVES
turns.text: I would say the bottom-line rule is Catholic --

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: Is that the bottom line?

turns.name: NICHOLAS R. REAVES
turns.text: The bottom line is, if it's a public benefit --

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: Your -- let's get to the bottom -- I'm asking you a direct question. Your Catholic schools will reject a child merely because their parents are homosexual?

turns.name: NICHOLAS R. REAVES
turns.text: I would say, if it's the sincere religious exercise of the Petitioner, then I think that would be permitted.

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: If it's a sincere religious exercise to exclude blacks, this principle would permit the exclusion of those black children?

turns.name: NICHOLAS R. REAVES
turns.text: No, Your Honor. And I -- I don't think that's the open --

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: Why? Because that belief would not be a genuine religious belief?

turns.name: NICHOLAS R. REAVES
turns.text: No, Your Honor. I think this Court --

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: How about national eth- -- national origin or ethnicity? There are some religions that are based on those protected characteristics.

turns.name: NICHOLAS R. REAVES
turns.text: Your Honor, I think, in all of these situations, you can compare what this Court said in Bob Jones to what this Court said in Fulton. Both of those cases reached strict scrutiny, and the difference was that the government said there is an overriding government interest, not just a compelling interest, an overriding interest.

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: That goes back to general applicability. I'm not --

turns.name: NICHOLAS R. REAVES
turns.text: Well, Your Honor, strict scrutiny would still apply here. We're not -- we're not saying this is just straight to we get to participate in the program. If the government is -- is excluding someone from a public benefit solely on account of their religious exercise, that would trigger strict scrutiny. And then the government can come forward and say we have a really good reason for this. And we just don't think they've done that in this case.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Justice Kagan?

turns.name: ELENA KAGAN
turns.text: You and Justice Alito just had a conversation about wouldn't the state legislature have to know that this was going to have an effect on Catholic schools. And that seems absolutely true, that they would presumably know that some Catholic schools would not wish to go along with the State's antidiscrimination policy in the same way that a state legislature that was passing a law against peyote use would know that there was going to be some religions that were going to be adversely affected by that law. So I think that that is not the question that our cases have suggested, that our decisions have suggested, whether you'd know. I mean, there are all kinds of generally applicable laws that you know adversely impact some group that disagrees with that law. I want to use peyote for religious purposes. The state says you can't. And the question, again, is, why doesn't -- why isn't that this case, where the state has a general antidiscrimination policy. Nobody can doubt the bona fide of -- bona fides of that policy. It is -- you know, it is -- it is not like this is another way to get at Catholic people. It's like we believe in antidiscrimination principles as applied to sexual orientation. And, you know, whatever we know about the schools that that will affect, that there are schools that will find it impossible to abide by that policy, we're not going to provide a special accommodation, which is what you're asking for, as opposed to those three cases that really were very different, where the religious institutions were just being asked to be treated the same.

turns.name: NICHOLAS R. REAVES
turns.text: Your Honor, I think the question at the end of the day is should this Court apply the Smith line of cases, which looks at it from the perspective of the government, or should it apply what I think Carson applied, which is it cited back to Sherbert and Thomas? Those cases look at the burden on religion from the perspective of the religious believer. So, in Thomas, the government defended its law in the same way. It said this is -- this law applies to everybody. In Sherbert, the government said everybody has to work on Saturday, whether you're religious or not. And Ms. Sherbert came back and said, well, my sabbath is the Saturday, and so I can't work on Saturday. This Court credited the religious --

turns.name: ELENA KAGAN
turns.text: But, if I may say, Mr. Reaves, I mean, the -- the -- the Sherbert analysis -- and we distinguished Sherbert in various ways over the years, but the old pre-Smith analysis was, look, if it adversely affected a religious group, then strict scrutiny had to apply. And Smith got rid of that analysis. And now you're saying, well, that analysis has to come back in full force because we once cited Sherbert in a case, you know, because Carson cited Sherbert in a case. But Carson upheld a very different principle, which was completely consistent with Smith, which was you can't treat religious institutions differently. That's not the principle that's at issue here. The principle at issue here is, do you have to treat them better?

turns.name: NICHOLAS R. REAVES
turns.text: Well, Your Honor, I think, at the end of the day, the question is, are Sherbert and Thomas still good law in the public benefits space? Because I don't take Smith to be overturning those cases. They distinguish those cases twice. And so, when it comes to conduct that the state has made unlawful, that's covered by Smith. But there's no question these Catholic schools can continue their teachings if they don't take this benefit. We think this is a coercive benefit, you know, a 20 percent decline in enrollment in these Catholic preschools. But my view is Sherbert and Thomas remain good law at least in the context of public benefits. And I think this Court's decision in Carson confirms that. And my -- my submission is I just don't see any difference between this case and those cases.

turns.name: ELENA KAGAN
turns.text: Thank you.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Justice Gorsuch?

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: Yeah. If everything turned on express discrimination as opposed to being more careful with your words, what would be left of Sherbert and Thomas?

turns.name: NICHOLAS R. REAVES
turns.text: I don't think much would be, Your Honor.

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: We'd have to overturn those, I would think, wouldn't we?

turns.name: NICHOLAS R. REAVES
turns.text: I think that's probably right, yes.

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: Yeah. And -- and can -- there's some amici that talk about what's happened in the wake of Carson. Can you talk about what your understanding is about how states have responded?

turns.name: NICHOLAS R. REAVES
turns.text: Absolutely. It's not just Colorado that's done this. In Maine itself, after this Court's decision in Carson, before the ink was even dry in Carson, Maine changed its laws to look more like the laws here, where they don't explicitly call out religion, but they still exclude the same families and the same schools. So I think there's no question that if this Court doesn't address the Carson issue here, you're going to have other states trying to do the same thing, trying to exclude religious schools, just without using religious terminology. I think that is a serious problem.

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: So Carson itself and Trinity Lutheran and Espinoza, we were just wasting our time for the last 10 years on those cases and -- as well?

turns.name: NICHOLAS R. REAVES
turns.text: Well, you know, I'm not the one to -- to say that, Your Honor, but I -- I think, you know, the -- I think Maine seems to think that. They seem to think they could get around it. I -- I tend to think that's the -- the situation.

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: The Constitution tends to deal in substances, not in shadows and procedures.

turns.name: NICHOLAS R. REAVES
turns.text: I -- I completely agree, Your Honor.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Justice Kavanaugh?

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: My understanding is that the Catholic preschools here do not categorically exclude students with parents in same-sex marriages for that reason alone, correct?

turns.name: NICHOLAS R. REAVES
turns.text: That is correct, Your Honor.

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: Okay. What -- and this may be outside the record, so say what you can. But Catholic schools around the country, there are definitely lots of Catholic schools with children who have parents in same-sex marriages, gay teachers, gay coaches, gay athletic directors, gay students. What -- of what relevance -- is that true? Of what relevance is that as we think about the issue here?

turns.name: NICHOLAS R. REAVES
turns.text: Your Honor, I don't doubt that that's true. At the end of the day, it's a question for the archbishop in -- in Denver to -- to decide on the religious teaching. And I think every diocese can make their own decision about where exactly that line is. The requirement to affirm the statement of community beliefs has been in place in the Archdiocese long before this program started. And I think it's -- it's their thoughtful attempt to say, we're creating a Catholic community, so we want to ensure that everybody who participates in the school, whether it's a parent who volunteers or whatever the situation might be, is acting consistent with -- with the responsibility we've been given as parents to teach these kids the Catholic faith.

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: Doctrinally now, you have two separate arguments as I see it. One is what you've called Carson/Sherbert -- Thomas. And your argument there, just picking up on Justice Kagan's question, as I understand your argument, it is that Sherbert, as to public benefits, survives Smith and that Smith was careful to actually carve out public benefits as different from an outright prohibition, and, therefore, the Sherbert principle that strict scrutiny is triggered when there's a substantial burden on religious exercise from a public benefit still exists as good law today?

turns.name: NICHOLAS R. REAVES
turns.text: That's correct.

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: Okay. Now that creates an anomaly, though, and I just want to give you a chance to explain it, which is raised in the Respondents' brief and in some of the amicus briefs. The anomaly is that you're imposing greater First Amendment scrutiny on a benefits program than you are on an outright ban on the religious conduct. And that seems inverted because, in a funding condition, the religious entity has the ability to decline the funding and still engage in the activity. In an outright ban, they don't have that ability, yet the doctrine as you set it up here would impose greater First Amendment scrutiny on the funding condition than the outright ban. Do you want to respond to that? I mean, one answer might be you'd say, well, you should just overrule Smith entirely. But assume that's not on the table in this case. Then how do you deal with that anomaly?

turns.name: NICHOLAS R. REAVES
turns.text: Yeah, two responses, Your Honor, one practical, and, hopefully, the second one, doctrinal, is more satisfying. The practical one is just that's what Smith did, as you described. And the concurrence in Smith makes exactly the same point. The concurrence says, why are we treating benefits better than direct prohibitions? And the majority doesn't respond to that. But the doctrinal answer, which I think will hopefully be more satisfying, is that if you look at it from the perspective of Smith, Smith is focused on the government's interest, and the government's interest is at its zenith when you're talking about criminal laws. Smith was concerned about every man becoming a law unto himself. It was concerned about having to give these broad exemptions to criminal prohibitions. That interest is not as strong when it comes to public benefits when the underlying conduct is lawful. One other way to just explain it is Smith looked at this from the government's perspective. Sherbert and Thomas looked at this from the religious believers' perspective. And I think that's one way to understand it. I would also point to what this Court said in Carson. In Carson, this Court made clear that when it comes to public benefits, you have to be particularly strict and look carefully at how the program is set up because it's really easy for the government to try to tweak the way the program works to kind of subsume the challenged condition within the scope of the program. You can't do that when it comes to criminal laws. There's the Rule of Lenity. There's other procedural protections that criminal defendants have. Just to give one more example, you know, in this case, after we filed our complaint, you know, at that time, the catch-all exception wasn't written into the regulations. It was just an online form. Preschools could submit the form and ask for an exception. There was no, you know, restrictions on it. This is in the record at JA 828. It was only on the second day of trial that Colorado introduced brand-new regulations trying to put restrictions on the catch-all exception to make it look more generally applicable. That's what this is -- that's what Smith is encouraging governments to do.

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: Right. And then you -- you're blending into this, but the whole second argument -- put aside Sherbert and Thomas and Carson -- is that even under Smith, it's not generally applicable because of all the exceptions, two in particular, but the whole slew of exceptions. Do you just want to spell that out as a distinct argument so that we -- succinctly?

turns.name: NICHOLAS R. REAVES
turns.text: Yeah. Succinctly, Your Honor, yes. Yeah, there's two main points under general applicability. The first is kind of our -- our broadest argument. This is just not the type of across-the-board, generally applicable law that Smith envisioned. This Court in Kennedy described what -- what it need -- what you need to have to have an across-the-board prohibition. And when you have, you know, all these different preschools getting to limit their enrollment in all these different ways, that's a problem. But then, even if you zoom in on the mandate specifically, which is where Colorado focuses, and that's what they pointed to when they said these Catholic schools are not allowed to participate, there are some problems there as well. So the one thing that Colorado has been consistent on throughout this case is that their government interest is in the mandate, enforcing the mandate uniformly. It's a hard limit. Even in their brief before this Court, at pages 41 and 51, they state their government interest, and it's just in enforcing the mandate regardless of the protected characteristic. At the same time, they let other preschools favor families based on those protected characteristics if there's a good or important reason. And I think it's telling that Colorado doesn't say, you know, we're not spending 10 pages of our brief kind of engaged in the work of statutory interpretation. They spend 10 pages explaining why it's really important to grant these secular accommodations.

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: Then --

turns.name: NICHOLAS R. REAVES
turns.text: And just to be clear, we agree those are important. We just want the same treatment.

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: Okay. So, even under Smith alone, you're saying strict scrutiny's triggered?

turns.name: NICHOLAS R. REAVES
turns.text: Yes, yes.

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: I guess the last question. You're expert in this area. What's the history of why Catholic schools developed in America? Again, succinctly.

turns.name: NICHOLAS R. REAVES
turns.text: Yes, Your Honor. Essentially, it was push-back on this common schools movement. So, in the late 1800s and early 1900s, there was real discrimination against Catholics and against Catholic beliefs. You had public schools, government-funded schools that were teaching the King James Bible and were not accommodating different Catholic beliefs. And -- and some of this is spelled out in the Barkley amicus brief as well. But, essentially, these Catholic schools were a response to their exclusion from the common school system.

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: Thank you.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Justice Barrett?

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: Mr. Reaves, I want to pick up on Justice Kavanaugh's point about the anomaly. Let's imagine that you win this case. So I guess the question is pressing you on, is there something special about public benefits? Let's imagine that you win this case, and so Colorado responds and says: Okay, now we're going to pass a law saying that all preschools, to have a license to operate, must comply with this EO kind of ban. What's your response to that law?

turns.name: NICHOLAS R. REAVES
turns.text: We'd be making different arguments. I don't think that would be a Carson case because I do think that's what this Court was addressing to some extent in Smith. It said --

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: So what would your arguments be in that case?

turns.name: NICHOLAS R. REAVES
turns.text: Well, I think we'd have to look at how the -- how the restriction was described, what it covered --

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: No exemptions? So is -- is -- in that case then, is it just you have to overrule Smith?

turns.name: NICHOLAS R. REAVES
turns.text: Well, I think, Your Honor, we'd still have church autonomy, the right of these schools to continue to inculcate the faith without government interference. There might be a parental rights Mahmoud argument. So I think there are other arguments we could make. I just don't think it would be a kind of Carson public benefits case.

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: Okay. Now my next question is about original meaning. We've been talking about this flowing from Carson, you know, this being a natural step from Carson. And it is true that Carson and Espinoza and Trinity Lutheran, all of those cases, and Sherbert, certainly apply strict scrutiny. Is that what you think is required by the original meaning, strict scrutiny? How do you see the relationship between the Sherbert test and the original meaning?

turns.name: NICHOLAS R. REAVES
turns.text: I think Sherbert is much closer to the original meaning than Smith, for sure. I don't -- I don't think the original meaning of free exercise of religion would -- would kind of care how the government treats non-religious groups or how the law is written. And I do think strict scrutiny in particular makes some sense if you look at these peace and safety provisos that lots of state constitutions had at the time. There was some understanding that, you know, we're going to protect the free exercise of religion up and to a -- up until a particular point, and that's when the government can come in and say we have this really important interest. I don't think peace and safety means anytime something's unlawful. It has to be -- you know, I think a close approximation is probably the strict scrutiny analysis this Court has adopted.

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: So you see it as an implementing doctrine that's close to how it would have been implemented at the time of the founding?

turns.name: NICHOLAS R. REAVES
turns.text: I think that's right, yes.

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: Okay. Last question is more of, I guess, a record question about how this developed. So you've gotten a number of questions about how it's hard to imagine that Colorado couldn't have seen this coming, I mean, especially given the history of disputes that have been in front of this Court between Colorado and religious entities, whether we're talking about bakers or web designers or -- or therapists are all in this case of religious objections to this kind of non-discrimination mandate in the case of traditional religious beliefs about sexuality and gender. But Colorado does say in its brief that the Archdiocese objections caught it by surprise, that they didn't see them coming. So I wondered -- which is, I guess, given the history that I just described, kind of surprising that they weren't caught -- that they say they weren't -- that they were caught by surprise. It's hard to see how this wasn't seen coming. But can you respond to that? You said that the preschool director of St. Mary's was part of the working group. Just -- just what exactly -- how did this unfold?

turns.name: NICHOLAS R. REAVES
turns.text: Yes, Your Honor. There's a few points there. So back in February, before this program started -- so it launched in August -- in February, the Archdiocese, as part of a coalition with Jewish schools and Lutheran schools, sought an accommodation. They raised the mandate and said, you know, we think this infringes on our religious exercise. They cited Trinity Lutheran and Espinoza. That's in the JA at 147 to 150. Colorado quickly responds and says, no, the mandate's a hard limit, we cannot accommodate you. Tracy -- Tracy Seul, who's the -- who was the preschool director, did participate in this religious working group. That's in the record at JA 233. And she raised these concerns. She said, for Catholic schools to participate, we might need this religious accommodation. Ms. Cooke's testimony at trial was that she understood their concerns went specifically to sexual orientation and gender identity.

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: But this was all after the mandate was passed. This was about implementing UPK?

turns.name: NICHOLAS R. REAVES
turns.text: This was after the statute was passed, Your Honor.

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: After the statute was passed.

turns.name: NICHOLAS R. REAVES
turns.text: While Colorado was working on the exception. So they had all these enrollment criteria that they were developing at the time.

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: I see.

turns.name: NICHOLAS R. REAVES
turns.text: So, yes, all of this is implementing the way the program operated. And I think the way that Colorado tries to explain why they were caught by surprise is because Catholic schools had participated in prior programs with somewhat similar nondiscrimination requirements, but, I mean, the record is clear that they're different in that they don't cover enrollment; they don't cover certain protected characteristics. So I think Colorado's argument is turning on the fact that there are some instances where Catholic schools have signed a nondiscrimination requirement. It's just not the same as this one. And I think it's even telling the district court in this case said it wasn't inconsistent for the Catholic schools to participate in those programs but to have a religious objection to UPK.

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: Thanks.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Justice Jackson?

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: So, I guess, going back to Justice Kagan's points, as I understand your Carson theory, it appears to threaten school funding programs, conditions, benefits, nationwide by giving religious entities and individuals a special preferred status. And I think her point and mine too is that that sort of takes this out of, at least conceptually, the Carson line, where it was clear that the Court was concerned about treating religious entities worse. Everybody else got access to this benefit, but the religious entity did not. Yet, here, it seems like you are saying the religious entity has to be treated specially. So let me give you a hypothetical. Suppose Colorado imposes certain educational standards on a school that receives state funding. As a benefit, you have to have certain educational marks; for example, the requirement that a student attains a particular level of proficiency in math. But a religious school might believe under its tenets that, say, female students aren't -- aren't allowed or shouldn't be allowed to learn math at all. Wouldn't your Carson theory require the state to exempt that school on the basis of their religious belief, even though that educational standard is being applied across the board and they're just -- they, the state, are just asking that condition of receiving this fund -- this funding is that this school, like every other school, teach math to all its students?

turns.name: NICHOLAS R. REAVES
turns.text: Your Honor, I think that would be a public benefit. So, under Carson, it would trigger strict scrutiny. The government could come forward and say we have a good reason and come forward.

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: But wouldn't it only strict -- wouldn't it only trigger strict scrutiny under Carson to the extent that it was treating the religious entity worse? That's my point. The strict scrutiny comes from the discrimination. And what I worry about in the way that you're framing this, sort of as a big picture, is that we've got two lines of precedent here that seem relevant to your claim. One says that when the state is handing out public benefits, it can't discriminate or disfavor religious entities. And that's Carson, Trinity, Espinoza. The other line says that if a state has a rule, but it's handing out exclusions, it's exempting people from that rule, then it can't refuse to do so for similar religious conduct. I think that this actually doesn't fit in either of those buckets, and that's what I'm worried about. I think you're asking us to do something more. In the first instance, this -- this religious entity would be treated better than everybody else who has to follow this rule. And in the second, the kinds of things you're talking about, the preferences that the -- Colorado has allowed is not similar. I mean, here, your schools want to discriminate by exclusion. Nobody else is allowed to do that. There's nothing in this record that shows that any other kind of school is allowed to discriminate by exclusion. I know, in theory, you know, some people might have testified. But that's not actually happening. And, certainly, the preferences aren't operating to discriminate by -- by exclusion. So why are you asking us to do something new and different in this case that certainly wasn't brought to the fore by these previous doctrines that, as I've described, are pretty narrow and make perfect sense?

turns.name: NICHOLAS R. REAVES
turns.text: Well, Your Honor, I wouldn't say what we're asking for is new and different. I think it's going back to Sherbert and Thomas, to what this Court has already said. The way you've described it is -- is similar. It's on all fours with Sherbert and Thomas. And I think that better reflects what the free exercise --

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: You disagree with -- with what Justice Kagan said and how some people have read the doctrine, which was that Smith actually displaced the Sherbert and Thomas concept of just because it burdens a religious activity, it gets strict scrutiny? You don't think that's right?

turns.name: NICHOLAS R. REAVES
turns.text: I don't think that's right when it comes to public benefits. And I think the language in Smith is telling. It says, you know, whether or not Sherbert and Thomas are limited, they at least have nothing to do with an across-the-board criminal prohibition on a particular form --

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: One final question. Doesn't Smith's concern about individuals and entities becoming a law unto themself arise if we interpret what you're saying? I mean, I understand you're trying to move Smith to the side, but it had some really serious concerns about religious entities not having to follow the law that everybody else is just because they hold sincerely held religious beliefs. It was like, how are you going to have a society where all people live and work together? And, here, we have a particular concern, as Justice Sotomayor pointed out, because what the religious entity would like to do is discriminate against a class of people. So we've got a conflict at some level between, like, the First Amendment right of the religious entity and potentially the Fourteenth Amendment right of certain individuals who would have the right not to be discriminated against. And so your -- your rule is, like, not allowing our society to have all people live together because it's preferencing the religious entity's ability to discriminate against others.

turns.name: NICHOLAS R. REAVES
turns.text: Well, Your Honor, our rule is the one that promotes pluralism. So these are private religious schools. They're not subject to the Fourteenth Amendment. But it's Colorado that's denying Catholic families equal access to this benefit also based on a protected characteristic, their religious exercise. And in terms of the practicalities of this case, 41 jurisdictions, including the federal government, are already subject to heightened scrutiny for any substantial burden on religion. And I think the federal government's probably the biggest provider of public benefits in the world, and they're functioning just fine.

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: Thank you.

turns.name: NICHOLAS R. REAVES
turns.text: You can also -- thank you.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Thank you, counsel. Ms. Harris. SUPPORTING THE PETITIONERS

turns.name: SARAH M. HARRIS
turns.text: Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court: There are two main paths to reversal. First, this Court could hold that public benefits programs that condition eligibility for benefits on foregoing otherwise lawful religious exercise trigger strict scrutiny. That's the rule Carson distilled from Sherbert, and that rule makes particular sense for educational benefits given the Court's longstanding recognition that religious education is vital to many faiths. Second, this Court could hold that Colorado's pre -- pre-K benefits regime triggers strict scrutiny under any approach because it isn't generally applicable. Either way, Colorado can't satisfy strict scrutiny. The better path in our view, though, would be to go with the first course, as Petitioner has emphasized. At this point, the doctrine is at a point where the Court should decide whether Sherbert survives. Carson puts that in sharp relief. And the Court's most recent decision in Mahmoud creates an especially untenable situation in the educational context because parents have strict scrutiny in this context and yet religious schools would not in many of the same claims. I welcome the Court's questions.

turns.name: CLARENCE THOMAS
turns.text: Would we have to extend Carson if we applied it?

turns.name: SARAH M. HARRIS
turns.text: I don't think you have to extend Carson for some of the reasons the Petitioner elucidated. While Carson itself emphasizes that it's an easy case in many ways because there is obvious discrimination on the -- on the face of the law for religious exercise, the reasoning, as was elucidated in some of Petitioners' answers to Justice Alito's questions in that colloquy, it's hard to separate out the reasoning of Carson saying that if you're sort of gerrymandering the law to be I'm not targeting religious exercise anymore, I'm saying anyone who subscribes to Catholic views of marriage gets excluded from benefits, you're kind of in the same boat. And I think the prefatory part of Carson makes absolutely no sense where the Court is giving the sort of full distillation of Sherbert, saying the rule of Sherbert that applies to public benefits is, if you force someone to forego public benefits as the price of religious exercise, that's no good. It's just hard to explain why the Court would have done that if that wasn't relevant to this context.

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: Counsel, your reasoning and Petitioners' reasoning would overrule Hastings College of Law versus Martinez, wouldn't it?

turns.name: SARAH M. HARRIS
turns.text: I think the --

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: That was a public benefits case, students receiving recognition and funding. And there, in a footnote, we dispensed with the claim that they could exclude members who weren't practicing, saying that the student group was seeking preferential, not equal treatment, and, therefore, it could not find support in the Free Exercise Clause.

turns.name: SARAH M. HARRIS
turns.text: So I think the Court -- there is absolutely tension with that footnote. I don't think it should bother the Court, and here is the reason. It was a drive-by ruling in a case that was mostly about free speech and associational issues, where the -- it was briefed in one page of the briefs, and the Court again dispensed with it in a footnote assuming and applying Smith without any examination of the threshold question, why is this a Smith case? I think it's very --

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: So we would have to overrule that footnote at least?

turns.name: SARAH M. HARRIS
turns.text: That footnote, I think, is hard to square, but I don't think it should trouble --

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: It is very hard to square. And we would have to overrule the limiting principle that Smith announced with respect to the Sherbert rule, correct?

turns.name: SARAH M. HARRIS
turns.text: I think the Court, in reciting a very different take on Sherbert and Carson, has already strongly suggested that, no, Sherbert cannot be cabined to the context of unemployment benefits where you look at the good cause exception. And, again, I think it's a little strange to suggest that that part of Smith has something for --

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: So let's go along with -- continue to go along with your logic. Your logic would suggest that a rule that said don't discriminate on the basis of ethnicity or national origin, if a religion requires a certain ethnicity, that group would have to be accommodated?

turns.name: SARAH M. HARRIS
turns.text: In -- no. That is not what we're saying. What we're saying is, in the public benefits context --

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: That -- this is a public benefits issue.

turns.name: SARAH M. HARRIS
turns.text: Right. I under -- but, again, in the public benefits context -- here's the limiting -- but here's how the analysis would run. You would ask, is there a substantial burden on religious exercise? And then, if there was, you would subject the rule to strict scrutiny. I think --

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: And under all circumstances, even though this rule says you have to accept everyone?

turns.name: SARAH M. HARRIS
turns.text: Yeah --

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: No exceptions, let's -- no exceptions, general applicability, you would say it's always subject to strict scrutiny?

turns.name: SARAH M. HARRIS
turns.text: In the context of this case, yes, our argument is no, the rule of Smith does not apply.

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: So that would be the same whether it's race, national origin, ethnicity, any protected characteristic? Sex seems to create the greatest difficulty because of the transgender and same-sex parents issue, but let's take it out of that.

turns.name: SARAH M. HARRIS
turns.text: Again, the Court crossed this same questioning in Fulton. The Court dealt with the same issue in Mahmoud. And I think the answer is there are certain areas where the burden on free exercise rights are such that yes --

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: Well, but we're not talking about changing what you teach, changing or requiring a changing of philosophy or belief. This is merely requiring people to accept anyone into their membership. What you're basically saying is we can exclude people merely because of exposure to them --

turns.name: SARAH M. HARRIS
turns.text: No.

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: -- would cause us harm. That's really what you're saying.

turns.name: SARAH M. HARRIS
turns.text: Respectfully, no. That elides --

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: That is completely what you're saying. We can exclude children of same-sex marriage. We can exclude children who are trans -- who might have transgender feelings or beliefs because exposing other children to them creates a problem.

turns.name: SARAH M. HARRIS
turns.text: No. The position in this case is that the religious exercise involved, as Petitioners spelled out, is requiring parents to agree with a school that they're going to adhere to tenets of the Catholic faith and act consistently with them to -- as a core part of performing --

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: The parents, not the child. You can still teach the child what you want.

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: Ms. Harris, can I -- oh, sorry.

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: No, go ahead.

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: I was just going to ask you to step back for a minute. You've been asked some questions about how this might play out with every person becoming a law unto himself or herself. So I just want to ask you as a practical matter, what other areas do you see in the public benefits context people seeking exemptions on the basis of faith and triggering strict scrutiny? And, of course, you don't necessarily survive the strict scrutiny. You didn't in Bob Jones. That religious entity did not. But what other exemptions do you anticipate or that you think you would see that would cause this, you know, we're going to devolve into everyone becoming a law unto himself?

turns.name: SARAH M. HARRIS
turns.text: I don't think there's a law unto themselves problem. And the experience of the federal government under RFRA and the 40 states that have RFRA equivalents, I think, is illuminating on this both in terms of understanding what a substantial burden on religious exercise looks like and in running the analysis under heightened or strict scrutiny.

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.name: SARAH M. HARRIS
turns.text: And so --

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: As a matter -- as a matter of statute, the federal government in provision of its many public benefits already has to meet strict scrutiny in a case like this, right?

turns.name: SARAH M. HARRIS
turns.text: That's right. And I think there's additional comfort from the pre-Smith line of cases. There's no law-unto-yourself problem. There is a refinement of the doctrine. So, again, the answers in those cases turned out both ways. Some laws flunked strict scrutiny, cases like Lee were accommodating religious exercise, for the Amish faith not paying taxes, for instance, would take the whole tax system down, and the Court reasoned you can't essentially say you have to modify the entire provision of the federal program in order to accommodate that. So I think the analysis really trains on what is the accommodation that's being sought, and would it compromise the government program at large?

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: But these --

turns.name: ELENA KAGAN
turns.text: Are public schools public benefits?

turns.name: SARAH M. HARRIS
turns.text: Yes, public schools are both public benefits. This Court said that in Mahmoud. There's also a compulsory --

turns.name: ELENA KAGAN
turns.text: So is the next case parents in a public school saying it's really important to my religious beliefs that my child not be educated with children of same-sex parents?

turns.name: SARAH M. HARRIS
turns.text: And we dealt with some of those hypotheticals in Mahmoud just in the argument. And I think the answer to that is similar to the answer I just gave Justice Barrett on how the inquiry runs on Lee. At the point when the accommodation proceeding --

turns.name: ELENA KAGAN
turns.text: And how -- the answer to that is basically that will be dealt with in the strict scrutiny part of the analysis, is that correct?

turns.name: SARAH M. HARRIS
turns.text: Yeah, and not only that, that's what the Court held in Mahmoud. Again, the claim you're envisioning --

turns.name: ELENA KAGAN
turns.text: I'm just trying to figure out what the answer. It's --

turns.name: SARAH M. HARRIS
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.name: ELENA KAGAN
turns.text: Right? I mean, it puts an enormous amount of pressure on that part of the inquiry, right? Everything becomes: Well, is this going to pass or is this going to fail strict scrutiny, which is a kind of balancing test, which is like how important is the state interest? How important is the religious belief? How do we compare the one to the other? Are they kind of apples and oranges and incomparables? I mean, I thought that in -- in some aspects of our jurisprudence, this Court has been trying to get away from that. And now you're saying, with respect to at -- with respect to religion, at least in public benefits cases, which include public school cases, everything is going to be about weighing religious beliefs against state interests in things like nondiscrimination but not limited to that state interest.

turns.name: SARAH M. HARRIS
turns.text: So a couple responses to that. One is just a conceptual response. I do think the threshold question of what constitutes a substantial burden is actually a really key sort of filtering part. And we talked about this in the Mahmoud argument a little bit. But there are questions that I think are harder than this one about whether -- in cases where you're not being forced to forgo a public benefit as the price of your religious exercise and there's sort of direct coercion involved, what does constitute a substantial burden?

turns.name: ELENA KAGAN
turns.text: Yeah, I mean, forgive me, Ms. Harris, but I think, given what we -- given the fact that this Court is never going to really question anybody's -- the sincerity of anybody's beliefs, it's going to be pretty easy for religious groups or religious individuals to come forward and say this would be a substantial burden on my religious belief or on my religious practice. That seems like, yeah, maybe, in once in a blue moon, you're going to have somebody fail that but not very often. So then, again, everything's going to be about how important is this religious belief to you versus how important is this interest here in nondiscrimination law to the state? And, again, that seems like an inquiry that the Court, like, ought to be thinking why would we put ourselves in the middle of that in -- in all these cases? With respect to public schools alone, these inquiries could go on forever.

turns.name: SARAH M. HARRIS
turns.text: So a couple responses. One, just to attack the strict scrutiny piece of it, a hundred percent. I think O Centro rightly recognized strict scrutiny. Even when people say it's tough, it is a very manageable standard for courts. It's a familiar standard for courts. It is a heck of a lot better than this situation with Smith, where you are going to be in an endless sort of whack-a-mole game of what's the state's asserted about interest? Can they reframe the asserted interest? What's a real secular comparator? How does that work? That is a much less stable jurisprudence. The jurisprudence of strict scrutiny, I think, has workable guideposts from the pre-Smith era. I think Lee on the one hand and Sherbert on the other hand are useful guides. And the idea that -- again, you're already in the thick of this with Mahmoud. And so I think it is truly perverse, especially in the public context, to have a situation where parents get strict scrutiny for their free exercise rights for many of the same laws that are at issue here, and yet schools are somehow subject to only rational basis review when they're subject to the same restrictions and might be co-plaintiffs in the same case. So I do think the Court should address that just stark disparity.

turns.name: ELENA KAGAN
turns.text: Thank you.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Thank you, counsel. Justice Thomas, anything further? Justice Alito? Justice Sotomayor?

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: The Amish case might have been easy because they didn't want to pay taxes. But how about the Bowen case, 1986? We rejected a free exercise challenge to a plaintiff who objected to using a Social Security number to receive welfare benefits. So is mere in -- administrative inconvenience a compelling state interest that supersedes the individual? Or will now every public welfare program have to accommodate every religion who doesn't want to use a Social Security number?

turns.name: SARAH M. HARRIS
turns.text: So I'm glad you brought up Bowen because I think there's two pieces of Bowen that are important. One is the holding that attracted a majority of the Court, which is you can't say that the government internally can't use Social Security numbers for its administration. You can't force a change in the way in which the government itself manages internal operations. The Court has said --

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: No. But they were forcing her to use a number she didn't want to give.

turns.name: SARAH M. HARRIS
turns.text: So the second part of Bowen is the part that fractured the Court. There's only a plurality of justices -- the -- the line-up ultimately was, were the case not full of jurisdictional defects on that question which got remanded, five -- at least five justices thought that if you are forcing someone to use a Social Security number in the actual application for benefits, that would trigger strict scrutiny under Sherbert. And, again, Bowen had the debate presaging Smith and talked about what does it mean under Sherbert. And a majority of the justices at that point said, no, the Free Exercise Clause is absolutely not limited to nondiscrimination. It -- it covers --

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: All you've done is prove the point that, no matter what line of cases we follow, there will be tremendous problems and a great cost to someone.

turns.name: SARAH M. HARRIS
turns.text: Respectfully, I disagree with the idea that there is no way out of this. I think the Court's cases point -- the timeline --

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: There is -- there is no way out of it because there's always balancing that goes on with these issues. But we have a clear line now, and you want us to just upend it in one particular area of all.

turns.name: SARAH M. HARRIS
turns.text: No. I think the Court currently has a mess. It is a Swiss hole doctrinal setup in which it is -- it's hard to describe Smith as a default, and it's even harder to describe Smith as a workable default in this particular context, not only because of the upshot of the Carson line but also because of what I just discussed about Mahmoud in the benefits context.

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: Because we created it.

turns.name: SARAH M. HARRIS
turns.text: Because the Constitution requires accommodation in this context.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Justice Kagan, anything? Justice Gorsuch?

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: I guess I'm struggling to see how it would be the end of the world or a sea change to just go straight to strict scrutiny here when the federal government has to anyway as a matter of statutory law under RFRA. That abrogated Smith for purposes of the federal government, and there are 40 states that already have to do this. That -- that seems to me to -- to be problematic to suggest, oh, my goodness, it would be a sea change to -- to do what -- what we do in almost every case.

turns.name: SARAH M. HARRIS
turns.text: I strongly agree with that and think that is a -- a very strong refutation to the idea that every person would be a law unto themselves. The law that is prevalent in so many contexts is already this.

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: I -- I think Senator Kennedy and Senator Hatch would be quite surprised to think that RFRA created laws unto themselves in every American.

turns.name: SARAH M. HARRIS
turns.text: No dispute.

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: Yeah. And then, in terms of strict scrutiny being a balancing test, that's -- that's not how I've understood it. The way I've understood it is we assess whether the government has a compelling interest and whether it's narrowly tailored to that interest without balancing against the interest on the other side. That's taken care of by saying the Constitution applies. There's a substantial burden once that hurdle's cleared. We don't go balancing the two. Is that right?

turns.name: SARAH M. HARRIS
turns.text: Yes. And I would just offer one refinement. Again, it is not just sort of balancing, is there a compelling interest on the one hand and a burden on religion on the other? The question, as this Court reiterated most recently in Fulton, is does the government have a compelling interest in denying the particular religious exception requested? And so that's what you're turning your analysis on for narrow tailoring and the governmental interest.

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: Right. We're focused on the government's interest once we're in strict scrutiny land and only the government's interest.

turns.name: SARAH M. HARRIS
turns.text: Yes.

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: Yeah. And then -- and then, just to follow up on Justice Barrett's question, do you think strict scrutiny as announced in Sherbert by Justice Brennan and -- and Thomas and then again in our series of public benefit cases more recently is -- is a reasonable construction of -- of the original meaning?

turns.name: SARAH M. HARRIS
turns.text: Yes. And I think just -- you know, I don't -- I don't need to tell this Court, but I think Justice Alito's distillation of many of the founding-era principles building on the backs of previous writings on the topic of the debates over Smith correctly captures the meaning of the public safety exception as something it can do strict scrutiny and helps explain the trajectory from the founding-era practice and the understanding that the Free Exercise Clause was not an outlier and the First Amendment was not the only thing limited to a mere nondiscrimination rule, all the way to when the Court started incorporating the Free Exercise Clause against the states, cases like Murdock, very early cases in incorporation, distill that very same principle, all the way through to Sherbert. And so, yes, I think that is a very faithful trajectory and applies with special force in the public benefits context. And that's why even Smith itself said the Court's not overturning Sherbert; it's keeping Sherbert, it's trying to cabin Sherbert, but it's not overturning that line of cases.

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: Thank you.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Justice Kavanaugh?

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: So just to pick up on that, as a matter of original meaning, you're saying that the Free Exercise Clause is more than simply a protection against explicit discrimination --

turns.name: SARAH M. HARRIS
turns.text: Yes.

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: -- against religious groups? On Sherbert, your view, I think -- I just want to make sure as a matter of doctrine and precedent -- is that Smith preserved Sherbert as to public benefits cases. Is that your -- your understanding?

turns.name: SARAH M. HARRIS
turns.text: Yes. I think that's how you have to read it or otherwise, as Justice Souter put it in his Lukumi concurrence, you have just a completely nonsensical understanding of what Smith was doing and overturning Sherbert without any analysis of stare decisis or what it was throwing overboard. Textually, it's also consistent with what Smith is saying about the critical importance in that case of the underlying criminal prohibition and how that "distinction" was critical for purposes of distinguishing the Sherbert line. So yes.

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: On strict scrutiny and when the government can win on strict scrutiny, in the oral argument in Fulton, the question about racial discrimination came up, and both the attorney for the religious group and the attorney for the United States said that the government has a compelling interest in eradicating racial discrimination going back to Loving and other -- many other cases and, therefore, would satisfy strict scrutiny in that case if a religious group tried to do that. Do you agree with that still?

turns.name: SARAH M. HARRIS
turns.text: I agree with that, and Pe a-Rodriguez, as -- as the government mentioned in Fulton, is a particularly good distillation of the particularly compelling interest in that context.

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: Back to Sherbert, any concerns or anything you want to add to your friend on the seeming disparity of greater scrutiny on a funding condition as compared to an outright ban?

turns.name: SARAH M. HARRIS
turns.text: I agree with both responses, that one, it's what Smith itself says and the only move that Smith could make to avoid overturning Sherbert entirely, and so I would point the Court to the -- the language about, you know, how many times criminal conduct is emphasized, the procedural posture of Smith itself. There's no sort of other way to read it. But I also agree with Petitioner, the more satisfying explanation is, why would you treat criminal prohibitions differently? It is because Smith was looking at it through the lens of the greater state interest in what Smith described as general applicable prohibitions of "socially harmful conduct." So the thinking is, when the government is trying to have a criminal law, the kind of conduct involved is in the government's judgment particularly pernicious for society, can't tolerate exceptions across the board is the thinking of Smith. And I think, if the Court wants to preserve that distinction, the Court doesn't have to say this is a great distinction, but it is certainly a distinction embedded in Smith itself and a line that is workable to draw.

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: And then last question. There's been some discussion of is this a favor or is this treating them equally or providing an accommodation, I guess another way to say it.
