So, if a Jewish service member is given Saturdays off, is that giving that service member a favor, or is that ensuring equal opportunity for that service member?

turns.name: SARAH M. HARRIS
turns.text: I think that is ensuring vindication of free exercise rights and something that that person is compelled to do. So I don't think it's like a special favor to people to respect a First Amendment right. I -- I disagree with the framing that there is some sort of impermissible thumb on the scale involved.

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: Thank you.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Justice Barrett?

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: Ms. Harris, I just want to have you say, let's imagine the federal government made it a condition of tax-exempt status to have the kind of nondiscrimination policy that Colorado has here, and the Catholic Church didn't want to sign on. Would you describe what would happen as a matter of RFRA?

turns.name: SARAH M. HARRIS
turns.text: Sure. As a matter of RFRA, the government would have to show -- again, it's just -- the question is, is there a substantial burden on religious exercise.

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: Mm-hmm.

turns.name: SARAH M. HARRIS
turns.text: And can the government -- and what's the government's compelling interest in -- in ensuring a uniform application of the tax code? And in denying that exception, I imagine we would rely on the Lee case quite a bit because it's on -- you know, very similar to that.

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: Sure.

turns.name: SARAH M. HARRIS
turns.text: And then the question is, is the government -- does the government have a compelling interest in not giving an exception in that context. So --

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: But it's the kind of law -- I guess my point here is it's the analysis that would apply in the federal government context.

turns.name: SARAH M. HARRIS
turns.text: Yes.

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: As Justice Gorsuch said, it's the analysis that would apply in 40 states.

turns.name: SARAH M. HARRIS
turns.text: Yes.

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: So it's something that's done in these other contexts and wouldn't be all that unusual.

turns.name: SARAH M. HARRIS
turns.text: No. It would be commonplace.

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: In fact, it would be the majority approach.

turns.name: SARAH M. HARRIS
turns.text: It's commonplace.

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: Yes. Thanks.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Justice Jackson?

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: But, of course, RFRA is a statute. You're talking here about what the Constitution requires with respect to the standards, right?

turns.name: SARAH M. HARRIS
turns.text: Absolutely. But, to the extent there are concerns about how workable is the standard, I think the Court should take great comfort from the fact that when you look about what the default rule is, it's not Smith in many, many, many contexts. It is the rule captured in RFRA.

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: Yes, workability. But there's also a concern about consistency with respect to what we've said about standards. I mean, it -- it seems to me that you're saying that regardless of whether a law facially targets religion or effectively singles out religion, strict scrutiny applies anytime it disproportionately burdens or unduly burdens a particular person's religious exercise. That's the test that you seem to endorse here, which sounds basically like a disparate impact rule for religious claimants. But we don't have that same standard operating under the Constitution in other First Amendment contexts. In the free speech context or equal protection cases, a law's disparate impact on the protected class this Court has said is not enough to trigger strict scrutiny. So I'm wondering again why it seems like in this religious context we have different standards operating?

turns.name: SARAH M. HARRIS
turns.text: I guess I would say a couple of things. One is with respect to disparate impact being a bit of a misnomer. I think the best way of looking at this is on almost an as-applied basis. The law that's applied to me is forcing me, coercing me to give up my free exercise rights. I am not allowed to engage in the free exercise religion in a very direct way. I am Adell Sherbert. I'm not allowed to hold my job.

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: No, but the law -- excuse me. The -- you can't have that operating, that concept operating consistent with the public benefits voluntary nature of this. I mean, I thought the entire thing was in the context of public benefits. The school itself does not have to admit anybody it doesn't want to admit. It can absolutely as a private entity discriminate and say we're not accepting these students, but if they're accepting public benefits voluntarily, these are the conditions that apply. So why is that forced to do anything?

turns.name: SARAH M. HARRIS
turns.text: Because, under the Court's line of cases, I mean, certainly, Carson reaffirms the idea, like, this is directly the framework I'm saying. When you are forced to forego public benefits as a price of engaging in a religious exercise, that is 100 percent a form of coercion of your religious beliefs. The courts recognize --

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: And you're saying that's not a disparate -- it doesn't operate in the same way as disparate impact?

turns.name: SARAH M. HARRIS
turns.text: It does not operate in the same way as disparate impact. And if you want to look at the other constitutional doctrines, I think Smith is the anomaly in the context of public benefits or in any other context, where other rights do not have this so long as a law is generally applicable rational basis review.

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: Let me ask you about -- let me -- let me -- let me just -- my time is short. Let me shift to the concern about the conflict here that when we're talking about the particular religious exercise that is at issue being one that potentially raises constitutional concerns on the other side. Here, the religious entity -- I understand there's something about making a statement with respect to it, but the bottom line is that the religious entity does not want to have to commit to opening its schools to students, children of LGBTQ couples. Couldn't that same logic support a religious entity who says we don't want to open our schools to students of races that we disagree with or ethnicities that we disagree with? Why wouldn't the same logic from the standpoint of the First Amendment claim be the -- be the same?

turns.name: SARAH M. HARRIS
turns.text: So a couple points on this. One is this goes back to the colloquy I just had with Justice Kavanaugh. In certain contexts, and this is already true in the RFRA context or in the Mahmoud context, where parents rights were involved, you can have the same kinds of claims, hypothetical sort of religious exercise involving race, involving other things. It will trigger strict scrutiny. And the answer I gave to Justice Kavanaugh is I think it is very possible, indeed likely, that the answer may well come out differently for strict scrutiny.

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: But that's just arbitrary. That's just because the Court would say race is different, right? I mean, that's -- there's no principled basis, I think, to distinguish between a entity that says my religious faith says my children can't go to school with the children of gay people from a religious entity that says my religion says my children can't go to school with the children of black people. And so what I'm trying to understand is, if we say that's different, it would just be because we've decided that race is different than LGBTQ status. But, from the standpoint of rational reasoning, understanding how the Constitution works, I'm not sure those are different.

turns.name: SARAH M. HARRIS
turns.text: So let me just back up. One -- just like go through the steps of the inquiry. One is, is there the same kind of substantial burden on religious exercise?

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: Yes.

turns.name: SARAH M. HARRIS
turns.text: Maybe if I'm --

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: Both of them sincerely believe that their children should not be in school with people of that character.

turns.name: SARAH M. HARRIS
turns.text: Right. So I think the intuition is at that level, perhaps you could survive that -- that -- in that hypothetical while the substantial burden part. But then you have to pivot to the strict scrutiny analysis. And I don't think it's just sort of a made-up doctrine in which you're asking which one is more important. I think it's --

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: And it's strict scrutiny just because they're a religious group and they sincerely -- that's what -- I'm just getting at that point. You say regardless, just because a religious group says I don't want to have to do whatever this standard is, we automatically pivot to strict scrutiny. That's where we are?

turns.name: SARAH M. HARRIS
turns.text: No. I think, in your hypothetical, you outlined, again, one -- a hypothetical that is not seen anywhere in the case law of these cases but a legitimate hypothetical with respect to assume that a particular religious faith says that I have you as a race that mean that, you know, I need to employ racially discriminatory admissions criteria.

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: Not so far-fetched. This was, in fact, a lot of what was said in the '40s and '50s. But go for it.

turns.name: SARAH M. HARRIS
turns.text: Absolutely.

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: Right.

turns.name: SARAH M. HARRIS
turns.text: But, as a -- as a modern-day issue, I think those cases the Court recognized -- Bob Jones is a great example of what that -- what that ultimately resulted in, which is a case in which the strict scrutiny applied and the law -- and the law --

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: But you're -- finally, you're saying Bob Jones doesn't -- wouldn't mean that these religious entities lose?

turns.name: SARAH M. HARRIS
turns.text: I'm saying the same thing I said to Justice Kavanaugh, which is, under the race hypothetical, I think that race -- under the compelling interest test would very likely come out differently. And the second thing I'm saying is I think just taking a step backwards, the idea that the answer to the race hypothetical should be preserve Smith in the maximum number of contexts is already refuted by other contexts. In the RFRA context, I don't think it's result -- again, the practical results issue of what has happened is not rampant racial discrimination or rampant numbers of groups claiming religious exceptions based on racial views. It is quite the contrary. And, again, the Mahmoud case raises the same sorts of questions with respect to parents' substantial burden on religious exercise.

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: Thank you.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Thank you, counsel. Ms. Norton.

turns.name: HELEN NORTON
turns.text: Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court: Colorado welcomes religious preschools to UPK. The only thing Colorado asks is that they comply with the same conditions that every publicly funded preschool must meet, religious and secular alike. UPK is neutral towards religion. Well before this Court's decision in Carson, Colorado made three key choices. First, it expanded free high-quality preschool to every four-year-old in the state, when before its predecessor program focused only on low-income and disabled children. Second, it replaced its public school-only approach with a public/private partnership that welcomes private schools, including religious schools that teach religious education. And, third, it holds all participating preschools to the same standards, including student-teacher ratios, class sizes, teacher training obligations, and equal opportunity. Under this program, faith-based preschools remain free to teach their religious beliefs, including their beliefs about sex or gender or marriage. Free to teach them while receiving public funding. Under this program, publicly funded preschools choose their curriculum. And families, regardless of their protected class status, choose what schools to attend. But families have no right to change a school's curriculum. Finally, UPK's equal opportunity requirements are generally applicable. The statute requires that disabled and low-income children receive additional and specialized services because having a disability or living in poverty directly interferes with those children's ability to benefit from preschool at all. UPK does not devalue religion by allowing preschools to remove these barriers. The judgment below should be affirmed. I welcome this Court's questions.

turns.name: CLARENCE THOMAS
turns.text: You ask us to employ the -- Smith in analyzing or addressing this case, but in our last two benefits cases, Espinoza and Carson, we did not use, even cite, Smith. Why would we do that in this case?

turns.name: HELEN NORTON
turns.text: Your Honor, I understand every case in the Carson trilogy to be an application of Smith and not a displacement of Smith. In each of those cases, the Court interrogated whether or not the state had engaged in religious discrimination, thus triggering strict scrutiny. I see that as an application of Smith and not its displacement.

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: Counsel, you agree -- I'm sorry, Justice Thomas. Were you finished? You agree, don't you, that Colorado could not say that Catholic schools or evangelical schools or orthodox Jewish schools were excluded from participation in the UPK program?

turns.name: HELEN NORTON
turns.text: Absolutely. They are welcome.

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: So explain -- you heard some questions along these lines a moment ago. Then explain what the difference is between that and then choosing to impose a condition that you know that those schools will be unable to agree to?

turns.name: HELEN NORTON
turns.text: Your Honor, there is no evidence of any animus or hostility in this case. Neither lower court found any such evidence. And, in fact, they held completely to the contrary, that UPK welcomes religious providers. Again, it chose to move to a program that included religious providers and treat them alike.

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: Well, does it have to be animus? I guess I'm not assuming animus or animus against religion, but if you know that the effect of choosing that requirement will push out those with a contrary belief, how is that different? Just as a logical matter. I mean, I see differences. I mean, I'm not -- I'm not saying that there's not a difference between calling religion out expressly on the text of the statute and imposing indirectly this independent kind of condition. But we do have, you know, this oped in the New York Times by Aaron Tang saying, hey, don't worry, there's this way that, after Carson, Maine and other states can achieve the same result, impose these non-discrimination requirements because all these religions that hold these traditional beliefs will then be unable to participate in these programs. So I think even if it's not what Colorado did here, don't we have to think about that in deciding this case and how it will affect other programs?

turns.name: HELEN NORTON
turns.text: Your Honor, it's -- it's absolutely true that states engage in religious discrimination and trigger strict scrutiny when they have the intent to disfavor religion, regardless of whether that intent is transparent or hidden. And here there is zero evidence of Colorado's intent. It started this program well before Carson, a program to welcome religious providers, while requiring equal opportunity. Well before Carson, it chose to include religious providers. Pretty much the first thing this brand-new agency did was convene a working group of faith-based providers that included St. Mary to solicit their input, to welcome their inclusion, and to try to respond to their feedback.

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: Do you know if, as a matter of fact, the equality mandate predated the opening to religious schools or was it done concomitantly, or where did -- when did the quality mandate come into play?

turns.name: HELEN NORTON
turns.text: Yes, Your Honor. The testimony at the trial, just looking at JA 20 -- 224 to 225, tells the story of UPK from the voters' approval of the initiative in 2020 and then two years of outreach to stakeholders and to the creation of a mixed delivery program with equal opportunity requirements. And that legislation was then finalized and introduced in January of 2022 and enacted into law in April of --

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: That was the opening, but in the previous iteration, you said this -- this existed originally just for public schools. Right? Before the opening?

turns.name: HELEN NORTON
turns.text: Public schools serving low-income kids and disabled --

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: Was there an equality mandate in place at that point, do you know?

turns.name: HELEN NORTON
turns.text: Yes. And, of course, they're constitutional actors, so --

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: Right. So the quality mandate predated the inclusion of these religious schools. It's not as though they chose that to preclude religious schools. At the time they chose it, religious schools weren't even in -- on the -- on the table, correct?

turns.name: HELEN NORTON
turns.text: You're -- you're absolutely right. Colorado has long been committed to equal opportunity in the educational setting of -- of all educational settings.

turns.name: SAMUEL ALITO
turns.text: Is there any --

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Counsel --

turns.name: SAMUEL ALITO
turns.text: Go ahead, chief.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: The effect of a law on religious schools and parents, I think the effect of the law in Carson is pretty much the same as the effect of the law here. And we said in Carson that it turned on the substance of free exercise protections. And I wonder in what way you think this is different than Carson.

turns.name: HELEN NORTON
turns.text: Yes, Your Honor. Carson is a religious discrimination case. It uses the terms "religious discrimination" 11 times. And if this -- if Carson stood for the proposition that Petitioners claim it did, this Court would have had no occasion to take the time and care that it did to explain that Maine was discriminating against religion when it excluded schools precisely because they taught religious things. In Carson, a state agency official examined the curriculum of applying schools, and if they found that curriculum to be religious in content, the school was excluded. That is religious discrimination. And that is not UPK.

turns.name: SAMUEL ALITO
turns.text: Do you think that Carson was in essence a Smith case? A Smith decision?

turns.name: HELEN NORTON
turns.text: I think it's an application of Smith's commitment to neutrality, yes.

turns.name: SAMUEL ALITO
turns.text: Did it cite Smith?

turns.name: HELEN NORTON
turns.text: It -- it did not cite it, but it did Smith's work. And I believe that any judicial decision when it is interrogating neutrality and when it's interrogating general applicability is doing Smith's work.

turns.name: SAMUEL ALITO
turns.text: Is there any evidence in the record of LGB -- LGBTQ couples wishing to enroll their children in Catholic pre-K schools?

turns.name: HELEN NORTON
turns.text: Yes, Your Honor. I'll start with the expert testimony, which was unrebutted and unchallenged and credited by the district court, which explained that same-sex parents, like religious parents, like all parents, often seek to place their children in schools that work best for their lives, regardless of the curriculum. In the record is the fact that one of the plaintiff preschools turned away a family of a fifth grader because the parents were same-sex. A number of the amicus briefs, by Colage and the National Women's Law Center, details the --

turns.name: SAMUEL ALITO
turns.text: And how many instances of this have there been?

turns.name: HELEN NORTON
turns.text: In -- sorry. I'm sorry. I didn't hear your question.

turns.name: SAMUEL ALITO
turns.text: How many times has this happened?

turns.name: HELEN NORTON
turns.text: So if we -- if we look at this particular situation, I want to remind us why we're here. We are here because the Petitioners declined to participate in the program and filed a pre-enforcement action asking for a blanket exception from the equal opportunity requirements. This in a program that was created because Colorado wanted to make certain preschools, all preschools, available to children that couldn't previously afford them. The fact that there aren't any complaints in the record is a feature of the fact that Petitioners have chosen not to participate and that -- and that -- the program's newness.

turns.name: SAMUEL ALITO
turns.text: Well --

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: How is -- I'm sorry.

turns.name: SAMUEL ALITO
turns.text: No.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: I was just going to say, how is any of that different than what happened in -- in Sherbert? The same background, it seems to me, applies in that case. And -- I -- I -- if you step back, it seems to me that you're quite anxious to bury Sherbert, perhaps as anxious as the other side is to bury Smith. And I'm just trying to be -- figure out the extent to which your problem is not the same as the problem that was in Sherbert, because nothing in our precedent has backed away from Sherbert. And I want to know exactly what -- how you fit under the analysis in Sherbert.

turns.name: HELEN NORTON
turns.text: Your Honor, Smith, which of course itself was a public benefits case, took care to explain Sherbert as a failure of general applicability, because there, in that case, the state had devalued religion by crediting secular and not religious reasons for refusing suitable work. I'll note that actually the Court in Sherbert also described it as religious discrimination because there the state had expressly protected workers that observed a Sunday Sabbath from having to work on that day even in times of emergency, but provided no such protection to workers who observed a Saturday Sabbath. This Court in Fulton, again, like in Smith, described Sherbert as a failure of general applicability, as devaluing religion by preferring secular but not religious reasons for the same choices.

turns.name: SAMUEL ALITO
turns.text: Do you disagree with the proposition that Justice Gorsuch mentioned that the Constitution generally does not allow a government entity to do indirectly what it is prohibited from doing directly?

turns.name: HELEN NORTON
turns.text: I agree that it is completely clear that the government impermissibly discriminates when it does so by stealth as opposed to doing so transparently. And, again, neither happened here.

turns.name: SAMUEL ALITO
turns.text: So when a state imposes a tradition -- a condition that it knows certain religions cannot accept that -- the only question that is presented is whether that was done with the -- with the intent to discriminate against those religions?

turns.name: HELEN NORTON
turns.text: Your Honor, this Court has never held that knowing the effect of an action establishes without more the government's intent to single out religion for disfavor, and such a holding would discourage government from the sorts of public/private --

turns.name: SAMUEL ALITO
turns.text: Well --

turns.name: HELEN NORTON
turns.text: -- partnerships we have

turns.name: SAMUEL ALITO
turns.text: -- suppose -- well, there are lots of hypotheticals in the briefs. I will just mention one. Suppose you imposed a requirement that all preschools must ban teachers from wearing head covering. Would that be permissible?

turns.name: HELEN NORTON
turns.text: All teachers cannot wear head coverings?

turns.name: SAMUEL ALITO
turns.text: Yes.

turns.name: HELEN NORTON
turns.text: So we would interrogate it under Smith for neutrality. We would need to know the background circumstances. And we would interrogate for general applicability. And we would need to know the government's asserted interest to assess those things.

turns.name: SAMUEL ALITO
turns.text: Well, let's -- let's say the government's asserted interest is a belief in gender equality, and it does not want women to wear head coverings because that is a symbol of unequal status.

turns.name: HELEN NORTON
turns.text: If it is neutral and generally applicable, then we go to rationality. And under some limited circumstances, it might fail rationality. But if it is neutral, and if it is generally applicable, it does not trigger strict scrutiny under the Free Exercise Clause.

turns.name: SAMUEL ALITO
turns.text: So we have here a -- a requirement that has a very severe impact on certain religions and that was something that everybody could have anticipated, and almost must have anticipated, when this requirement was imposed. And we have little evidence of a practical problem, little evidence, if any evidence -- you'll tell me if I'm wrong -- that there are LGBTQ couples who cannot find other preschools to send their children to. And we have your state's record in recent First Amendment cases to which Justice Barrett referred, Chiles versus Salazar last term, violating -- violation of the free -- First Amendment rights of the Christian counselor; 303 Creative in 2021, violation of the First Amendment rights of a Christian website designer; Masterpiece Cakeshop in 2015, violation of the First Amendment rights of the Christian baker. What should we make of all of this?

turns.name: HELEN NORTON
turns.text: Your Honor, there is no evidence of any sort of any religious hostility or animus in the UPK program. Neither lower court found any such evidence. And, in fact, they found exactly to the contrary. Colorado here has made several choices, choices they didn't need to make that were all about opening this program to religious people and religious providers.

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: Why not seek the win/win? I mean, I raised this in the Fulton oral argument where there's a clash of rights, obviously, the free exercise right on the one hand, and same-sex marriage right recognized in Obergefell on the other, but there are 2,000 schools. There are only 34 Catholic schools. There are plenty of opportunities to respect the rights of the religious believers and respect the ability of LGBT parents to find among the 2,000 schools appropriate fit for their children, which could, in fact, be at one of the Catholic preschools, depending on their own beliefs about that, and you avoid the clash. It seems like this is a -- you know, a would-be solution in search of a problem that is unnecessary to create this clash. And I'm just trying to figure out why -- why we're here, why this problem has risen all the way -- I had the same question in Fulton. Why -- why has this been provoked when there's an ability for everyone to go to the school, a good school that's a fit for them and respect religious rights? Maybe I'm wrong in my premises. You can tackle that, as you wish.

turns.name: HELEN NORTON
turns.text: Thank you, Your Honor. One distinction I will draw -- there is several distinctions between this case and Fulton. One distinction that I will draw is that it is clear in this case, based on the unrebutted expert testimony, that preschools are not interchangeable to families. That was not the case in -- in Fulton. There wasn't any evidence of the different placement agencies were different. So Colorado's interest is ensuring that it's public funds go to schools that ensure equal opportunity, not some opportunity, that ensure equal opportunity to public-funded options, regardless of protected class status. Families are harmed when they're turned away from the publicly-funded schools that makes their lives work because of the protected class status. Think of the parent who needs a school that opens at 7:00 a.m. so she can get the bus that takes her to work. Think of the parent who needs a school that will take all three of her kids, so she doesn't have to shuttle them among three different schools. Think of the parent who needs the neighborhood school so that her neighbor can pick up her school -- her kids when she can't get home in time. For that parent to be turned away from those schools that make preschool possible for her family because of her protected status -- class status, harms families and undermines --

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: What do you --

turns.name: HELEN NORTON
turns.text: -- Colorado's interest.

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: -- do with all the other preferences that are in Colorado law? There are dozens and dozens of applications of preferences. For example, I notice one preference that's allowed, schools are allowed to have a preference for parents who will be more involved in the school.

turns.name: HELEN NORTON
turns.text: Yes.

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: That almost inherently discriminates against single-parent families, inherently discriminates against families with two-income parents in the real world. You know, don't you have the same problem with something like that? Or you have the STEM school that, you know, someone is interested in something else, they are not going to -- they are going to be going to a different school or the vegetarian school, you can have a vegetarian school, but you can't have a Catholic school, you can't have a Jewish school. What do you -- how do you respond to those concerns, which you have seen in the briefs? I just want to give you an opportunity.

turns.name: HELEN NORTON
turns.text: Thank you, Your Honor. UPK does not regulate schools' enrollment criteria, so long as they don't violate the equal opportunity requirements. And none of the preferences that you -- or have been discussed so far, none of them departs from the equal opportunity requirements. This is a very familiar feature of equal opportunity law in the educational setting. So, for example, Title VI, which regulates federally-funded schools, it takes three characteristics off the table; race, color, national origin, and it literally leaves federally-funded schools thousands of other enrollment criteria that they can -- they can continue to -- to use and implement. UPK allows no exceptions from its equal opportunity requirements.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Could the preschools spend 80 percent of their time teaching religion?

turns.name: HELEN NORTON
turns.text: Yes.

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: I just want to go back to Justice Alito's question about whether there was any record of any LGBTQ parents being turned away. I understand that this is a preenforcement challenge, and so the Catholic preschools haven't participated in the UPK program. But -- and maybe I'm misremembering. I guess my question here is, is there any record -- I mean, these preschools preexisted the program. So is there any record of those -- of same-sex parents, say, trying to attend these Catholic preschools and being turned away?

turns.name: HELEN NORTON
turns.text: There's -- I gave you the example of the fifth-grader.

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: Well, a fifth-grader is not pre-K, right?

turns.name: HELEN NORTON
turns.text: But it was by a plaintiff school with a -- with a preschool.

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: So turned away. That was the fifth-grader, was that St. Mary's?

turns.name: HELEN NORTON
turns.text: St. Bernadette.

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: St. Bernadette. Who is not in the case anymore, right?

turns.name: HELEN NORTON
turns.text: Correct.

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: And is there any other entity -- I guess this kind of goes to Justice Kavanaugh's point about why are we here. Is there any entity, other than the religious entities, who sought an exemption from the equal opportunity mandate?

turns.name: HELEN NORTON
turns.text: No, Your Honor. But I want to go back to your earlier question, which I also understand to be related to some of the other questions about -- about why are we here? And I sense folks -- perhaps their puzzlement about whether or not same sex parents would even want to send their children here. And I -- I've talked earlier about the expert testimony that says that same -- same-sex parents often rely on location and hours more than curriculum in making their choices. And we can see other examples of this sort of behavior. For example, in Bob Jones that you mentioned earlier, Black students -- some Black students attended Bob Jones despite their religious teaching on race. If you go to Zelman versus -- to the Zelman case here, the religious preschools that were participating in that voucher program, the -- the record made clear that most of the students that attended those religious schools did not agree with those schools' teaching but, nevertheless, sent their kids there because of the quality of the education. The bottom line is allowing the Petitioners a blanket exemption to turn families away because of protected class status limits the publicly funded options for those parents. And they experience harm when they don't have the full range of choices as other families.

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: I can understand that. I think the thing that I'm struggling with -- and, again, this kind of goes to Justice Kavanaugh's point -- is in the racial discrimination cases -- and again, Bob Jones triggered strict scrutiny and then it failed. I mean, the school wasn't allowed to continue to maintain the interracial dating ban. But I guess what I'm struggling with here is those -- those cases, there was a problem that they -- the laws were responding to about racial discrimination in these institutions. So I guess what the question was getting at is, is Colorado trying to eradicate that kind of problem in the schools, does that problem exist anywhere, except among the religiously committed schools that are plaintiffs in this case? What -- what is it responding to? It's just hard for me to imagine that this is -- this kind of discrimination is -- is a problem in Colorado and that you could be responding to anything else, other than the religious schools.

turns.name: HELEN NORTON
turns.text: Your Honor, with respect to any protected characteristic, certainly sexual orientation, but also race or sex, there might be religious reasons for turning families away on those bases, but often there are instead secular reasons. Unfounded stereotypes about membership in that group. Fear of folks who are perceived as different. And with respect to same-sex parents, maybe unfounded fears of HIV trans- -- transmission. Maybe secular beliefs, personal beliefs, political beliefs about the appropriate structure of the family. Drawing lines on the basis of protected class status is by no means motivated only by religious reasons. And UPK's requirements regulate the conduct of denying equal opportunity regardless of the religious or sexual motivation for that.

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: Does Colorado --

turns.name: ELENA KAGAN
turns.text: I think one aspect of the questions that you've been getting just now is to ask you to comment on why Colorado has an exceptionally important interest in the uniform application of antidiscrimination law. You know, is there anything about antidiscrimination law that makes it particularly wrong to begin to make exceptions here or another place or another place and say that, you know, some people in our society don't really have to follow its strictures?

turns.name: HELEN NORTON
turns.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honor, and especially so in the context of public funding, when a state is making decisions about how to spend the public's funds. And, again, it goes back to Colorado's interest, which is in equal opportunity, not some opportunity. And I want to talk a little bit about this and -- and what the Petitioners' approach to strict scrutiny would mean with respect to other types of -- of protected class status, including interracial parents. Religious beliefs that are very, very different from Petitioners' belief but absolutely whatever approach that you adopt here will apply to religious beliefs very different from Petitioners'. Petitioners say that even if a state has a compelling interest, the state fails narrow tailoring if it refuses to grant the exception, so long as some school somewhere will take those parents. That would be true of same-sex parents here. That would be true under that logic of interracial parents as well.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Well, it's --

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: Are single --

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: I was just going to say, your answer there, it seems to me to be a question of the application of strict scrutiny. And we've heard today there are situations where, historically, in recent times, strict scrutiny has been found to be satisfied.

turns.name: HELEN NORTON
turns.text: Thank you -- thank you, Your Honor. And my point is that under Petitioners' application of strict scrutiny, it would not be.

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: Are -- are -- does Colorado allow single-sex preschools?

turns.name: HELEN NORTON
turns.text: Yes.

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: And why?

turns.name: HELEN NORTON
turns.text: Sex is not one of the characteristics enumerated in the UPK law. It's not unlike Title II or Title VI, which lists some characteristics and not others. States frequently focus on some characteristics in their equal opportunity laws, and they have the constitutional latitude to do so, so long as they take care to make sure their law is neutral and generally applicable as is assuredly the case here, where Colorado protects religion among its characteristics.

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: Wouldn't -- wouldn't Colorado's exemption for single-sex preschools have some of the effects on parents' geographical location, hours, et cetera, that you mentioned before?

turns.name: HELEN NORTON
turns.text: Your Honor, there's nothing in the record about why sex wasn't included, but the free exercise inquiry, again, focuses on those requirements and whether or not they --

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: My -- my -- I'm sorry to interrupt. My question was, wouldn't some of the impacts on parents that you described earlier be true as well if -- given Colorado's allowance of single-sex preschools? If you have daughters and the closest preschool is all boys, you know, that's going to be a hindrance. Why does Colorado allow that?

turns.name: HELEN NORTON
turns.text: So I know of no equal opportunity law that takes every possible decision-making criteria off the table. Colorado also doesn't identify parents' age as a protected characteristic or their veterans status. You could -- you could certainly -- you're not wrong, Your Honor, but my point is that legislatures frequently have to decide. They don't want to --

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: They have to draw lines. On -- on the -- different question now, just -- and this is a clash of rights and strong beliefs and strong interests. And I get -- I completely understand that. One of the things that Obergefell and Masterpiece were very careful to say, though, that in recognizing a constitutional right to same-sex marriage, that the Court was also respecting the rights of people, particularly religious people who had religious beliefs that were different, and that it was important going forward as a country to make sure both rights were respected.

turns.name: HELEN NORTON
turns.text: Yes, Your Honor. Absolutely. And Colorado funds Catholic schools. Colorado funds Catholic schools that teach Catholic precepts. Colorado does not interfere and, in fact, funds teaching Catholic views on family and sex and marriage. The next sentence in Obergefell, Your Honor, goes on to say that however well intentioned those beliefs, the dangers of -- of law that demeans or stigmatizes or includes -- excludes some folks based on protected characteristics.

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: So it sounds like you're -- you're sort of making a distinction in response to Justice Kavanaugh, that is we have this clash of rights and we're trying to accommodate both, but to the extent that -- sorry -- and to the extent that a state is doing things that discriminate against a religious entity on the basis of their religion, then we're on the line, we're on the line of the -- the state can't do that. But we have a little bit of an odd scenario here when the religious belief at issue is compelling the exclusion of others, and the others have a concomitant, one would say, right to be included. And so I'm just a little concerned about the state being in a very precarious position here, because it, it seems to me, has this well-established interest in making sure that all low-income students have access to pre-K regardless of these -- the characteristics that it -- it has identified. That seems pretty unobjectionable in -- in -- you know, on its face. And the question is why wouldn't, Judge -- Judge Kavanaugh -- Justice Kavanaugh asks, the state yield that concern in a situation in which a religious group says but we don't want to include certain people?

turns.name: HELEN NORTON
turns.text: Your Honor, I think that choice is -- is particularly acute in the public funding context. The Smith framework, the yield of the Smith framework is that when states take the care to design their programs in a neutral and generally applicable way, then they have the constitutional latitude to choose whether and when to exempt religious actors and to choose whether and when those requirements, those neutral and generally applicable requirements, brook no departure. And, here, Colorado has chosen that -- that -- the idea that it's going to invest the public's funds, the people's funds, to provide services to the people only in schools that ensure equal opportunity regardless of these characteristics.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Thank you, counsel. Justice Thomas? Justice Alito?

turns.name: SAMUEL ALITO
turns.text: In answer to Justice Kagan, I recall your saying that there is a greater need to allow no exceptions based on religious beliefs in -- in antidiscrimination laws than in other laws. Is that correct? Do you want to say that? That's an area where Smith applies most emphatically?

turns.name: HELEN NORTON
turns.text: Yeah, what -- what I intended to say, Your Honor, that it is -- it is a longstanding and commonplace and strong interest of states to ensure that they invest their public funds in entities that do not deny equal opportunity. And that's been recognized in Lau versus Nichols and Gebser and Bob Jones and --

turns.name: SAMUEL ALITO
turns.text: I'm just trying to understand you. So -- and you also seem to say that there's a greater interest in applying Smith in public benefits cases than in other cases. Is that what you just said?

turns.name: HELEN NORTON
turns.text: No. I just think that there's -- there's -- it's particularly appropriate to apply Smith. I don't think it's limited to public benefits cases.

turns.name: SAMUEL ALITO
turns.text: And antidiscrimination cases, there's a stronger need to do it there than, let's say, in the criminal law?

turns.name: HELEN NORTON
turns.text: No, I don't think so, Your Honor. I -- I was answering a question about whether or not this was -- that why Colorado was choosing, because Smith gives it the right to choose so long as it is neutral and generally applicable, choose not to exempt religious actors from this requirement. And it's because, among other things, a commitment to equal opportunity should mean equal opportunity and not some opportunity.

turns.name: SAMUEL ALITO
turns.text: We've heard a lot of praise for a blanket rule limiting free exercise to nondiscrimination. Is it not the case that the application of that rule across the board would itself have consequences that are pretty hard to accept?

turns.name: HELEN NORTON
turns.text: Tell me more.

turns.name: SAMUEL ALITO
turns.text: Well, I mean, I'm not going to argue here today that Smith should be overruled. That was an issue in Fulton, and the Court did not choose to go down that route. But I did outline in that concurrence the consequences of saying Smith applies in all circumstances. Do you -- do you recall that, or do you want me to refresh your memory? One of the things it would allow is our imposition of a rule that says nobody could stand where you stand now with his or her head covered. So Orthodox Jewish men and many Muslim women's -- women would not be allowed to argue here. It would allow a rule that says that every slaughterhouse must render the animal unconscious before being killed, which would outlaw kosher and halal slaughterhouses, which is done in some European countries. It would mean that an -- a governmental entity could prohibit circumcision, which is also done in some European countries.

turns.name: HELEN NORTON
turns.text: Your Honor, I want to -- thank you, Your Honor. I want to make one point about the work that Smith does, and I want to make one point about the dangers of adopting a rule like Petitioner proposes, which would be an enormous inroads on Smith. Over the 36 years since this Court decided Smith, this Court has carefully developed both its neutrality inquiry from Lukumi through the Carson trilogy and also its general applicability inquiry, again, from Lukumi through Fulton. These now provide robust protections for religious exercise. These are serious screens for the government's religious discrimination. These are serious screens for the government's devaluing of religion. As a result, in the time since Smith, religious challengers prevail much more often than they lose before this Court when, in the period from Sherbert up until Smith, religious challengers lost considerably more than they won. Second, to adopt Petitioners' proposed gaping exception in Smith --

turns.name: SAMUEL ALITO
turns.text: Thank -- thank you, counsel. Thank you. You've answered my question. Thank you.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Justice Sotomayor?

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: Finish your answer.

turns.name: HELEN NORTON
turns.text: Thank -- thank you, Your Honor. To adopt Petitioners' proposed rules would subject -- would require -- create a standing entitlement of claimant-specific strict scrutiny to every neutral and generally -- generally applicable condition to public funding. This not only discourages public and private partnerships of the sort like UPK; it also introduces unfairness as some providers will be entitled to funding on terms unavailable to anyone else, and children in this case will be denied participation because of their parents' protected class status. It's divorced from precedent and it's unnecessary because Smith provides the -- the tools you need to decide this case.

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: Thank you.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Justice Kagan? Justice Gorsuch? Justice Kavanaugh?

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: One factual question. Under -- and I'm familiar with the record and how this transpired in the district court and what happened in the -- in the wake of that, but, under current Colorado law as it stands today, am I right that a religious school, preschool, can't prefer members of the same religion?

turns.name: HELEN NORTON
turns.text: Under UPK, a publicly funded preschool would violate the UPK statute if they turned folks away because of their religious affiliation, and Petitioners seek an exemption from that.

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: Right, but the -- the current law on even co-religionists, so a Jewish preschool, under current law as it stands today in Colorado, couldn't say we want to have a Jewish preschool and for predominantly Jewish children? You can't do that right now as a Jewish preschool or a Muslim preschool or a Catholic preschool, is that correct?

turns.name: HELEN NORTON
turns.text: If you receive UPK funding.

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: Okay. And then, second and last -- and I appreciate the program and the importance of the program and -- and what it does for children in Colorado -- I have one question. The director of the program, by all accounts, a dutiful public servant, but was asked at -- at the trial, "are you aware that Catholics have historically been discriminated against," and she answered no. I was surprised by that answer and curious if that's Colorado's position.

turns.name: HELEN NORTON
turns.text: Not at all, Your Honor. And it's Colorado's position that the equal opportunity requirements help religious families. They ensure that Catholic families are not turned away from the UPK school that best meets their needs because of their faith or because of any other protected characteristic. And a history of discrimination against Catholics is among the reasons that requirement is so important.

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: Thank you.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Justice Barrett?

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: Ms. Norton, I just have one question and it's a clarification of how this law works. I had been asking Mr. Reaves this, and I'm not sure that I quite have it pinned down. What if St. Mary's participated in the UPK program and committed to not turning away any families based on parents' protected status but said any parents that enroll their child in this program must sign a statement agreeing to support in every way the church's teachings on same-sex marriage, including that means not both attending events so that we don't have to explain to the other children the nature, you can come one at a time, but you can't both come, and in every respect support and never criticize the teachings of the church on faith? I kind of understood and I might have misunderstood Mr. Reaves to say that Colorado's program would permit that so long as the school didn't turn away children of same-sex couples, but I -- I'm not sure that that's right. Is that --

turns.name: HELEN NORTON
turns.text: I'm not sure either, Your Honor, and this is -- this is why. We're -- we're here, of course, because Petitioners filed a pre-enforcement lawsuit seeking a blanket exemption. They didn't ask us to say --

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: Well, would you allow what I just said? Would that be okay?

turns.name: HELEN NORTON
turns.text: This is what we would need to know. It's -- for sure, for sure, any school could ask parents to agree we are -- we are receiving -- we understand we're receiving Catholic teaching. We're taking -- we're sending our kids to a Catholic school. That -- that is an easy question for me. It's harder for me to figure out how that policy works without facts on the ground, and, in fact, CDEC wouldn't try to figure that out unless and until they got a complaint from a family and they could interrogate the effects on the ground to figure out how is this working, is it intentionally include -- excluding folks based on religious affiliation or some other protected characteristic? And, if so, does it rise to denying equal opportunity? That's the sort of inquiry Title IX and Title VI do all the time.

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: That makes sense. I -- I didn't quite understand how that worked. And your answer makes sense. Thank you.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Justice Jackson?

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: Very quickly, I just wanted to touch on the Tandon line of argument here. Does Colorado's preference program undermine the equal opportunity mandate or discriminate in a similar way as what these preschools would like to do?

turns.name: HELEN NORTON
turns.text: Could you tell me -- I didn't hear the first part of your question.

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: I'm sorry. I was just saying, I'm -- I'm trying to understand if -- if the preferences that they point to as a -- as something that Colorado allows, is that similar to what they want to do such that they have a valid Tandon argument here?

turns.name: HELEN NORTON
turns.text: Thank you, Your Honor. First, Colorado allows no departures from the equal opportunity requirements. To the extent that the Petitioners have argued that allowing Head Start providers to provide specialized services to low-income children or allowing school districts to provide specialized services to kids with disabilities, to the extent that they argue that the departure of equal opportunity requirements, they are wrong. Schools advance equal opportunity when they recognize that a child with a visual impairment needs different treatment in order to learn. Schools advance equal opportunity when they understand that kids in poverty can't learn if they're hungry or because they're in pain because their parents can't afford dental care to treat their cavities. Colorado advances equal opportunity when it allows these schools to bring -- give those children specialized services because they have a protected characteristic that impairs their ability to benefit from preschool. And this understanding of equal opportunity is consistent also, not only with the text, but also with 50 years of legislative and judicial precedent, as we explain in III.A of our brief.

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: Thank you.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Thank you, counsel. Rebuttal, Mr. Reaves?

turns.name: NICHOLAS R. REAVES
turns.text: Thank you, Mr. Chief Justice. First, a few factual points. There were a few questions about the record and the history of this case. I would first direct the Court to 306a in the Petition Appendix. That's where it talks about the fact that these Catholic schools were licensed for decades and there was not a single complaint of -- of anyone being excluded or turned away based on LGBTQ status at all. In addition, if we're talking about access to these preschools, I actually think the fifth grade example, which my friend on the other side pointed, to supports our position. The testimony at trial in that case was that this family came to the school, they met with the principal, they learned about the school's beliefs, and at the end of the day, it was a mutual decision that this was not the right fit for that family. That's the only example that's in the record. We also looked into it. And there are two UPK preschools currently in the program today within three miles of every single Catholic preschool in the Archdiocese. This is just not really a problem in real life. And -- and Colorado's own expert said any harm was speculative. That's at JA 419. And in terms of, you know, what actually happened in this case, this case went to trial. This is not a -- a PI rushed up to this Court. We had a trial. Our witnesses testified to what the Catholic church believes. Our witnesses testified, the preschool directors testified, the principal testified. So Colorado knows the facts. On JA 147, there's testimony that we submitted a -- an application. One of the Catholic preschools submitted an application to the program explaining what the religious beliefs are, and Colorado did not respond. So we've tried to participate in this program. A couple additional points. You know, when the state violates the Constitution, there might be multiple problems with what the state is doing. And I think that's what you see in Carson. In Carson, there's certainly a neutrality analysis, but I don't take that to be the only problem. And I think the first half of this Court's opinion makes that clear. In addition, Colorado cannot co-opt a religious school just because they think they provide a good education or an education that might be a good fit for certain families. That's this Court's decision in 303 Creative. In terms of the strict scrutiny analysis, I don't think you need to say anything more than you already said in Fulton. This is an even easier case than Fulton in terms of the strict scrutiny analysis. At the end of the day. I also think what Sherbert said about neutrality is right. When talking about the preference or the accommodation that was given in Sherbert, this Court didn't say it was -- this Court disclaimed the fact that it was -- the idea that it was establishing a religion. It said, instead, this is an obligation of neutrality in the face of religious differences. That's how you should think about accommodating religion. If someone is -- is -- is different, differently situated because of their religion, an accommodation is neutrality. In terms of, you know, what this case is about at the end of the day, I also think it's important to keep in mind that this is an as-applied challenge seeking to protect the religious beliefs that this Court called decent and honorable. And the people actually being excluded or being denied are families. It's -- it's Dan and Lisa Sheley, who are out $18,000 because of their religious exercise. Thank you.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Thank you, counsel. The case is submitted.
